framework: AP Precalculus Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2026)
subject: Precalculus

outcomes.text: Describe how a function's inputs and outputs vary together by comparing function values.
Define function, domain, range, independent and dependent variables, and when two functions are equal.
Know a function rule can be graphical, numerical, analytic or verbal; understand image and preimage.
Recognize a function as increasing on an interval when larger inputs always give larger outputs.
Recognize a function as decreasing on an interval when larger inputs always give smaller outputs.
Build a graph of two quantities that vary together in a real situation.
Know a graph shows input-output pairs and how the values vary together.
Use a verbal description of how things change together to build a graph.
Identify concave up where the rate of change is increasing.
Identify concave down where the rate of change is decreasing.
Know the graph meets the x-axis at zeros, where output is zero.
Compare rates of change at two points using average rates of change near them.
Define the average rate of change over an interval as output change divided by input change.
Approximate the rate of change at a point using average rates over small intervals around it.
Compare rates of change at two points using small-interval average rates.
Describe how two quantities vary together at different points and over different intervals.
Know rates of change measure how two quantities vary together.
Read a positive rate of change as both quantities moving in the same direction.
Read a negative rate of change as one quantity rising while the other falls.

topics.title: 1.3 Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions

subtopics.title: Average rates for linear and quadratic functions

outcomes.text: Find average rates of change for sequences and functions, including linear and quadratic.
Know a linear function has a constant average rate of change.
Know a quadratic function's average rates over equal-length intervals form a linear function.
Interpret the average rate of change over [a, b] as the slope of a secant line.

subtopics.title: Change in the rates of change

outcomes.text: Find how average rates of change change for linear, quadratic and other functions.
Know a linear function's average rates change at a rate of zero.
Know a quadratic function's average rates change at a constant rate.
Link increasing average rates to concave up and decreasing average rates to concave down.

topics.title: 1.4 Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change

outcomes.text: Identify key features of polynomial functions related to rates of change.
Define a polynomial function, its degree, leading term and leading coefficient.
Identify local and global maxima and minima where a polynomial switches between increasing and decreasing.
Know a local extremum lies between every two distinct real zeros.
Know even-degree polynomials have a global max or min, found at the vertex for quadratics.
Locate points of inflection where concavity changes.
Identify key features of polynomials related to zeros when factorizations or technology are available.
Define zeros, roots and linear factors, and link real zeros to linear factors.
Define multiplicity; a degree-n polynomial has n complex zeros counting multiplicity.
Link real zeros to x-intercepts and to endpoints of polynomial inequality intervals.
Know non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
Know even-multiplicity zeros keep the output sign and make the graph tangent to the x-axis.
Find the degree of a polynomial from constant successive differences of outputs.
Decide whether a polynomial function is even or odd.
Know even functions are symmetric over x = 0 with f(-x) = f(x).
Know odd functions are symmetric about the origin with f(-x) = -f(x).
Describe end behavior of polynomial functions.
Describe outputs as inputs increase without bound, using limit notation.
Describe outputs as inputs decrease without bound, using limit notation.
Use the degree and sign of the leading term to determine end behavior.
Describe end behavior of rational functions.
Define a rational function as a quotient of polynomials comparing numerator to denominator size.
Find end behavior from the quotient of leading terms.
Find a polynomial end behavior or slant asymptote when the numerator dominates.
Find a horizontal asymptote at a constant when neither polynomial dominates.
Find a horizontal asymptote at y = 0 when the denominator dominates.
Use limit notation for horizontal asymptotes.
Find the zeros of rational functions.
Know real zeros of a rational function come from real zeros of its numerator within the domain.
Use zeros of numerator and denominator as endpoints or asymptotes for rational inequality intervals.
Find vertical asymptotes of graphs of rational functions.
Locate vertical asymptotes at denominator zeros that are not cancelled by the numerator.
Describe behavior near a vertical asymptote with one-sided limit notation.
Find holes in graphs of rational functions.
Know a hole occurs where the numerator's zero multiplicity is at least the denominator's.
Find a hole's location from outputs near the input, using limit notation.

topics.title: 1.11 Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions

outcomes.text: Rewrite polynomial and rational expressions in equivalent forms.
Use factored form to read zeros, intercepts, asymptotes, holes, domain and range.
Use standard form to read end behavior.
Use information from different forms of the same function to answer contextual questions.
Divide polynomial functions using long division.
Rewrite f as g times quotient plus remainder, with remainder degree below the divisor.
Use long division to find slant asymptote equations.
Rewrite repeated products of binomials using the binomial theorem.
Expand (a + b)^n using a row of Pascal's Triangle, including (x + c)^n.
Build a function that is an additive or multiplicative transformation of another function.
Translate vertically with g(x) = f(x) + k.
Translate horizontally with g(x) = f(x + h), a shift by -h.
Dilate vertically with g(x) = a f(x), reflecting over the x-axis if a is negative.
Dilate horizontally with g(x) = f(bx), reflecting over the y-axis if b is negative.
Combine transformations; distinguish preimage from image.
Know a transformed function can have a different domain and range from its parent.

topics.title: 1.13 Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation

outcomes.text: Choose a suitable function type to model a scenario.
Model roughly constant rates of change with linear functions.
Model roughly linear rates of change or symmetric data with a single extremum using quadratics.
Model area situations with quadratics and volume situations with cubics.
Model data with several zeros or extrema using polynomials.
Model data with roughly constant nonzero nth differences using degree-n polynomials.
Fit a polynomial of degree n or less through n + 1 points with distinct inputs.
Use piecewise-defined functions when behavior differs over different intervals.
Describe assumptions and restrictions in building a function model.
State what a model assumes stays consistent.
State what a model assumes about how quantities change together.
Restrict the domain using mathematical clues, context or extreme data values.
Restrict the range, for example by rounding, using clues, context or extreme values.
Construct linear, quadratic, cubic, quartic, degree-n or piecewise models.
Construct a model from restrictions found in the mathematical or real context.
Construct a model by transforming a parent function.
Construct a model with technology and regression, including linear to quartic.
Construct a piecewise model by combining modeling techniques.
Construct a rational function model from a context.
Model inversely proportional quantities with rational functions.
Apply a function model to answer questions about data or a context.
Use a model to draw conclusions and predict values and rates of change, with sensible units.

topics.title: 2.1 Change in Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences

outcomes.text: Express arithmetic sequences as functions of the whole numbers.
Know a sequence is a function on the whole numbers whose graph is discrete points.
Recognize a common difference as a constant rate of change.
Write the general term a_n = a_0 + dn, or a_k + d(n - k).
Express geometric sequences as functions of the whole numbers.
Recognize a common ratio as constant proportional change.
Write the general term g_n = g_0 r^n, or g_k r^(n-k).
Contrast arithmetic growth (equal steps) with geometric growth (growing steps).

topics.title: 2.2 Change in Linear and Exponential Functions

outcomes.text: Build real-number functions comparable to arithmetic and geometric sequences.
Compare f(x) = b + mx to arithmetic sequences: initial value plus repeated constant addition.
Write a linear function from a slope and a point, as f(x) = y_i + m(x - x_i).
Compare f(x) = ab^x to geometric sequences: initial value times repeated constant ratio.
Write an exponential function from a ratio and a point, as f(x) = y_i b^(x - x_i).
Know sequences and their matching functions may have different domains.
Describe similarities and differences between linear and exponential functions.
Tell constant change (linear) from proportional change (exponential) over equal-length intervals; the ratio is not 0 or 1.
Compare linear (addition-based) and exponential (multiplication-based) forms built from an initial value.
Know two distinct values determine an arithmetic or geometric sequence, linear or exponential function.
Identify key features of exponential functions.
Know the form f(x) = ab^x, growth when a > 0 and b > 1, decay when 0 < b < 1.
Know natural-number inputs count factors of the base; the domain is all real numbers.
Know exponential functions are always monotonic and concave one way, with no extrema or inflection points.
Recognize functions modeled by an additive transformation of an exponential.
Describe end behavior and the asymptote at zero using limits.
Rewrite exponential expressions in equivalent forms.
Use the product property for exponents; horizontal translations equal vertical dilations.
Use the power property for exponents; horizontal dilations change the base.
Use the negative exponent property.
Read b^(1/k) as the kth root of b.

topics.title: 2.5 Exponential Function Context and Data Modeling

outcomes.text: Build a model for situations with proportional outputs over equal-length input intervals.
Use exponentials for patterns of repeated multiplication of a constant.
Add a constant to the data when needed to reveal proportional growth.
Build a model from a ratio and initial value or from two input-output pairs.
Build models by transforming f(x) = ab^x.
Build models with exponential regression technology.
Recognize the natural base e (about 2.718) as a common base.
Use exponential models to answer questions about data or a context.
Read the base as a growth factor tied to percent change.
Use equivalent forms to reveal different properties, such as growth per day versus per week.
Predict dependent values and solve for independent values, within domain limits.
Build linear, quadratic and exponential models from a data set.
Model slightly changing rates of change with linear, quadratic or exponential functions.
Compare models using context and applicability to choose the best.
Validate a model built from a data set.
Use residuals and residual plots; a model fits if the residual plot shows no pattern.
Interpret model errors, including over- and underestimates, in context.
Evaluate the composition of two or more functions for given values.
Define the composite f o g, its domain restrictions, and f(g(x)) notation.
Evaluate compositions from graphs, tables, formulas or words.
Know composition is not commutative.
Know the identity function leaves compositions unchanged.
Build representations of the composition of two or more functions.
Use composition to relate quantities with no direct formula.
Write f(g(x)) by substituting g(x) for x in f.
Build numerical or graphical compositions from values (x, f(g(x))).
Rewrite a function as a composition of simpler functions.
Decompose analytic functions into simpler pieces, replacing the variable properly.
See translations as composition with g(x) = x + k.
See dilations as composition with g(x) = kx.
Find the input-output pairs of a function's inverse.
Know a function is invertible when each output comes from a unique input; restrict domains to make it so.
Treat the inverse as a reverse mapping: pairs (a, b) become (b, a).
Find the inverse of a function on an invertible domain.
Know a function composed with its inverse gives the identity.
Swap domain and range, and reverse table pairs, to get the inverse.
Reflect the graph over y = x to get the inverse graph.
Find the inverse algebraically by swapping x and y and solving.
Know context can restrict where an inverse applies.
Evaluate logarithmic expressions.
Define log_b c as the exponent a with b^a = c; common log is base 10.
Evaluate some logs by arithmetic and estimate others with technology.
Read logarithmic scales as multiplicative steps of the base.
Build representations of the inverse of an exponential function with initial value 1.
Know the general form f(x) = a log_b x.
Contrast exponential growth (additive input, multiplicative output) with logarithmic growth (multiplicative input, additive output).
Know log_b x and b^x are inverse functions.
Graph the log as a reflection of the exponential over y = x.
Swap ordered pairs (s, t) to (t, s) between the exponential and its log.
Identify key features of logarithmic functions.
Know the domain is x > 0 and the range is all reals.
Know logs are monotonic and concave one way, with no extrema or inflection points.
Recognize logs as functions whose shifted forms have inputs proportional over equal output intervals.
Describe the vertical asymptote at x = 0 and unbounded end behavior.
Rewrite logarithmic expressions in equivalent forms.
Use the product property; horizontal dilations equal vertical translations.
Use the power property; powers on the input are vertical dilations.
Use the change of base property.
Define ln x as log base e.

topics.title: 2.13 Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities

outcomes.text: Solve exponential and logarithmic equations and inequalities.
Use exponent properties, log properties and inverses to solve.
Check solutions for extraneous values ruled out by domain or context.
Use logs to rewrite exponential expressions, including b^x = c^(x log_c b).
Build the inverse for exponential and logarithmic functions.
Invert f(x) = ab^(x+h) + k by reversing its operations.
Invert f(x) = a log_b(x + h) + k by reversing its operations.

topics.title: 2.14 Logarithmic Function Context and Data Modeling

outcomes.text: Build a logarithmic function model.
Use logs for proportional-growth situations where inputs change proportionally over equal output steps.
Build a log model from a proportion and a real zero, or two input-output pairs.
Build log models by transforming f(x) = a log_b x.
Build log models with logarithmic regression technology.
Recognize the natural log as useful in real-world modeling.
Predict dependent values and find independent values with a log model.
Decide whether an exponential model fits by examining a semi-log plot.
Know a log-scaled y-axis makes exponential data look linear.
Know linear log-output trends justify transformed exponential models without shifting the data.
Linearize exponential data.
Apply linear modeling techniques to a semi-log graph.
For y = ab^x, use the line y = (log b)x + log a, with slope log b and intercept log a.
Build graphs of periodic relationships from verbal descriptions.
Recognize a periodic relationship as outputs repeating over successive equal-length input intervals.
Build a periodic graph from one cycle.
Describe key features of a periodic function from a verbal description.
Define the period as the smallest positive k with f(x + k) = f(x).
Estimate the period by finding where the output pattern repeats.
Know every characteristic in one period appears in every period.
Find sine, cosine and tangent of an angle using the unit circle.
Place angles in standard position; use positive and negative rotation and coterminal angles.
Define radian measure as arc length divided by radius.
Define sine as the vertical displacement ratio, the y-coordinate on the unit circle.
Define cosine as the horizontal displacement ratio, the x-coordinate on the unit circle.
Define tangent as the slope of the terminal ray, sine over cosine.
Find coordinates of points on a circle centered at the origin.
Write the terminal-ray point on a circle of radius r as (r cos t, r sin t).
Use special triangles and quadrant signs to find exact values for multiples of pi/4 and pi/6.
Build representations of sine and cosine using the unit circle.
Define sin t as the y-coordinate of the unit circle point, with domain all reals.
See sine oscillate between -1 and 1 as the angle grows.
Define cos t as the x-coordinate of the unit circle point, with domain all reals.
See cosine oscillate between -1 and 1 as the angle grows.
Identify key features of sine and cosine.
Define sinusoidal functions as transformations of sine; cosine is sine shifted by pi/2.
Treat period and frequency as reciprocals; the period of sine and cosine is 2 pi.
Define amplitude as half the max-min difference.
Find the midline as the average of max and min.
Know sinusoids alternate between concave down and concave up.
Know sine is odd and cosine is even.
Identify amplitude, vertical shift, period and phase shift of a sinusoid.
Recognize the form a sin(b(t + c)) + d, with the same transformations for sine and cosine.
Treat adding d as a vertical translation that moves the midline.
Treat adding c inside as a phase shift of -c units.
Treat the factor a as a vertical dilation that changes amplitude.
Treat the factor b as a horizontal dilation that changes period.
Read amplitude |a|, period 2 pi/|b|, vertical shift d and phase shift -c from the form.

topics.title: 3.7 Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling

outcomes.text: Build sinusoidal models of periodic phenomena.
Estimate period and frequency from consecutive maxima or minima.
Find amplitude and vertical shift from the maximum and minimum.
Estimate phase shift by comparing an actual data pair to the model.
Build models with technology by estimating key values or using sinusoidal regression.
Use sinusoidal models within their contextual domain to predict values and solve for inputs.
Build representations of tangent using the unit circle.
Define tan t as the slope of the terminal ray.
Write tan t = sin t / cos t where cosine is nonzero.
Describe key features of tangent.
Know tangent has period pi.
Locate vertical asymptotes at pi/2 + k pi.
Know tangent increases and switches from concave down to concave up between asymptotes.
Describe additive and multiplicative transformations of tangent.
Treat adding d as a vertical translation of the graph and its inflection line.
Treat adding c inside as a phase shift of -c units.
Treat a as a vertical dilation, reflecting over the x-axis if negative.
Treat b as a horizontal dilation that changes the period, reflecting over the y-axis if negative.
Read the form a tan(b(t + c)) + d: dilation a, period pi/|b|, shift d, phase shift -c.
Build equations and graphs of the inverses of sine, cosine and tangent on restricted domains.
Know inverse trig functions swap input and output, giving an angle from a trig value.
Name arcsine, arccosine and arctangent, invertible only on restricted domains.
Use the standard restricted domains for sine, cosine and tangent.
Solve equations and inequalities involving trigonometric functions.
Use inverse trig functions to solve, adjusting solutions for domain restrictions.
Expect infinitely many solutions because of periodicity.
Use context to restrict the domain and limit the solutions.

topics.title: 3.11 The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions

outcomes.text: Identify key features of functions made from quotients of sine and cosine.
Define secant as the reciprocal of cosine.
Define cosecant as the reciprocal of sine.
Find vertical asymptotes of secant and cosecant, with range (-inf, -1] or [1, inf).
Define cotangent as the reciprocal of tangent, or cos over sin.
Know cotangent has asymptotes where tangent is zero and decreases between them.
Rewrite trig expressions in equivalent forms using the Pythagorean identity.
Derive and use sin^2 t + cos^2 t = 1 from the unit circle.
Rearrange the Pythagorean identity into other forms, such as tan^2 = sec^2 - 1.
Rewrite trig expressions in equivalent forms using sine and cosine sum identities.
Use the sum identity for sine.
Use the sum identity for cosine.
Use the sum identities to get difference and double-angle identities.
Verify new identities using known identities and algebra.
Solve equations using equivalent analytic forms of trig functions.
Choose equivalent trig forms that make information easier to access.
Use equivalent forms to solve trig equations and inequalities.
Locate a point using both rectangular and polar coordinates.
Define polar coordinates (r, t), including negative r and multiple names for one point.
Convert polar to rectangular with x = r cos t and y = r sin t.
Convert rectangular to polar using r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) and an arctangent, adjusted for quadrant.
Treat a complex number as a point in the plane, in rectangular or polar form.
Build graphs of polar functions.
Graph r = f(t) with angles as inputs and radii as outputs.
Restrict a polar function's domain by choosing endpoints of angle and radius.
Relate input changes to angle changes and output changes to signed radial displacement.

topics.title: 3.15 Rates of Change in Polar Functions

outcomes.text: Describe features of polar function graphs.
Know the distance to the origin grows when r is positive and increasing or negative and decreasing.
Know the distance shrinks when r is positive and decreasing or negative and increasing.
Find relative extrema as the points closest to or farthest from the origin.
Define the average rate of change of r with respect to the angle as signed radius change per radian.
Use average rate of change of r to estimate values in an interval.

units.title: Unit 4: Functions Involving Parameters, Vectors, and Matrices

outcomes.text: Build a graph or table for an analytically given parametric function.
Define parametric equations: x and y both depend on a parameter t.
Write the pair as one function f(t) = (x(t), y(t)).
Make a table of values by evaluating x and y at several t.
Sketch the graph by joining points in order of increasing t.
Know restricted domains give start and end points on the graph.
Identify features of a parametric motion function related to position.
Use f(t) = (x(t), y(t)) to model a particle's position at time t.
Find horizontal and vertical extremes from the max and min of x(t) and y(t).
Link zeros of x(t) to y-intercepts and zeros of y(t) to x-intercepts.

topics.title: 4.3 Parametric Functions and Rates of Change

outcomes.text: Identify features of parametric motion related to direction and rate of change.
Read direction from x(t) and y(t): right or left, up or down.
Know direction at a point can differ for different t.
Know one curve can be parametrized in different ways and directions.
Find slope between two points as the ratio of average rates of change of y and x.
Express motion around a circle or along a segment parametrically.
Model a full counterclockwise unit-circle revolution as (cos t, sin t) for 0 to 2 pi.
Transform (cos t, sin t) to model any circular path.
Parametrize a segment from one point to another using a start point and rates of change.
Build a graph of an equation involving two variables.
Know a two-variable equation can implicitly describe one or more functions.
Graph an equation by finding its solutions.
Solve for one variable to define a function that is part or all of the graph.
Determine how the two quantities in an implicit function vary together.
Read positive ratios of change as both increasing or both decreasing, negative as opposite.
Know a zero rate of change marks vertical or horizontal intervals.
Represent conic sections with horizontal or vertical symmetry analytically.
Write parabolas as x - h = a(y - k)^2 or y - k = a(x - h)^2.
Write ellipses as (x-h)^2/a^2 + (y-k)^2/b^2 = 1; a circle is a = b.
Write hyperbolas opening left-right or up-down, with asymptotes y - k = +/- (b/a)(x - h).
Represent a curve in the plane parametrically.
Check a parametrization by substituting x(t), y(t) into the equation.
Parametrize y = f(x) as (t, f(t)), and an inverse as (f(t), t).
Represent conic sections parametrically.
Parametrize a parabola by solving for one variable and setting the other to t.
Parametrize an ellipse with x = h + a cos t and y = k + b sin t.
Parametrize hyperbolas using secant and tangent.
Identify features of a vector.
Define a vector's tail, head and magnitude.
Write a plane vector as component form <a, b> from two points; know the zero vector.
Find direction and magnitude from components.
Use trigonometry to find components of a geometric vector.
Find sums and products involving vectors.
Multiply a vector by a constant to get a parallel vector.
Add vectors by adding components, tail-to-head.
Compute the dot product as the sum of component products.
Find a unit vector for a given vector.
Divide a vector by its magnitude to get a unit vector.
Write <a, b> as a i + b j with unit vectors i and j.
Find angles between vectors and magnitudes in vector addition.
Link the dot product to magnitudes and the cosine of the angle; zero means perpendicular.
Use the Law of Sines and Law of Cosines for triangles from vector addition.
Represent planar motion with vector-valued functions.
Write position as p(t) = <x(t), y(t)>; its magnitude is distance from the origin.
Use v(t) = <x'(t), y'(t)> for velocity; its magnitude is speed.
Find the product of two matrices.
Define an n by m matrix as n rows and m columns.
Multiply matrices when columns of the first match rows of the second, using row-column dot products.

topics.title: 4.11 The Inverse and Determinant of a Matrix

outcomes.text: Find the inverse of a 2 by 2 matrix.
Define the identity matrix.
Know multiplying by the identity leaves a matrix unchanged.
Know a matrix times its inverse is the identity.
Compute a 2 by 2 inverse with or without technology.
Apply the determinant to invertibility and vectors.
Compute det(A) = ad - bc for a 2 by 2 matrix.
Read the absolute determinant as the area of the parallelogram spanned by the vectors.
Know a square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.
Find output vectors of a linear transformation using a 2 by 2 matrix.
Define a linear transformation: each output component is a sum of constant multiples of input components.
Know a linear transformation maps the zero vector to the zero vector.
Write vectors as 2 by 1 matrices and sets of n vectors as 2 by n matrices.
Know every linear transformation has a unique 2 by 2 matrix, L(v) = Av.
Transform n vectors at once by multiplying A by a 2 by n matrix.
Link a linear transformation to its matrix.
Associate the map (x, y) to (a11 x + a12 y, a21 x + a22 y) with its matrix.
Use images of the unit vectors to find the matrix.
Use the rotation matrix to rotate vectors counterclockwise by an angle.
Read the absolute determinant as the area scale factor.
Find the composition of two linear transformations.
Know a composition of linear transformations is linear.
Multiply the matrices to get the composition's matrix.
Find the inverse of a linear transformation.
Know inverse transformations compose to give back every vector.
Use the inverse matrix A^-1 for the inverse transformation.
Build a matrix model of transitions between two states.
Turn percent change rates into a transition matrix over discrete steps.
Apply matrix models to predict future and past states.
Multiply the transition matrix by the state vector to predict future states.
Repeat multiplication to find the steady state.
Multiply by the inverse matrix to predict past states.
